policy: Reviewed founding programmes and field consolidation, not generic remit or the birth of entire fields. Existing dates protected; two explicitly reviewed missing publication starts filled. Applied after immutable bibliography and founding-001.

sources.title: Feminist Studies, institutional history
sources.note: History page read: organizing discussions from 1969, first publication in 1972, scholarly and political purposes, and early connections with the Berkshire Conference on the History of Women. Retrospective institutional account.

sources.title: Signs, A History of the Journal
sources.note: Institutional history read, including the reproduced 1975 editorial statement on new scholarship about women and its interdisciplinary aims. Not a separate full reading of the original first issue.

sources.title: Anne E. C. McCants, Editor’s Introduction to Volume 40, Issue 1, Social Science History (2016)
sources.note: Publisher text read: 1976 first volume and the founding SSHA constitution printed there, stating a programme of improving historical explanation through selective use of social-science theories and methods.

sources.title: Richard Trainor with Aris Grivokostopoulos, Whatever happened to social history?, Economic History Society centenary project (2026)
sources.note: Society’s historical research post read: first-issue economic-and-social subtitle and Ashley’s 1927 programme. The society’s 1926 establishment is separate from the journal’s 1927 publication start.

sources.title: Oral History Association Newsletter 7(2), June 1973, announcement of the new Oral History Review
sources.note: Read the launch notice: new annual Review combining papers from the 1972 Austin colloquium with contributed articles, distributed to members. This establishes a publication mechanism for the association’s field, not a claim about all later methodological positions.

sources.title: David Henige, On Method: An Apologia and a Plea, History in Africa 1 (1974), 1–7
sources.note: Publisher’s substantial opening extract read, not the entire seven-page article. The first-volume editor explicitly gives the new journal a methodological purpose: critical evaluation of sources and their use. DOI 10.1017/S0361541300005751.

sources.title: Antoinette Burton, Some origins of gender history as a field, Gender History: A Very Short Introduction (2024), chapter 1
sources.note: Publisher abstract read, not the chapter or the 1989 founding editorial. It explicitly identifies the 1989 launch and the journal’s purpose of examining gender’s historical experience, meaning and significance.

sources.title: Robert Rotberg interview with Ed Freedman, Fifty years of the Journal of Interdisciplinary History, MIT Press (2019)
sources.note: Publisher interview with the founding editor read: social-science and innovative historical methods, with a special place for quantification but a programme also encompassing art, climate and other approaches.

sources.title: Gerald Holton, George Sarton, His Isis, and the Aftermath, Isis 100(1) (2009), 79–88
sources.note: Read discussion of Sarton’s founding programme, dated November 1912 and published in volume 1 in 1913, together with the distinction between the initial synthesizing project and later pluralism. DOI 10.1086/597571.

sources.title: Sylvia L. Thrupp, Editorial, Comparative Studies in Society and History 1(1) (1958), 1–4
sources.note: Opening pages 1–3 read: comparative research across history, humanities and social sciences, communication between specialists, and attention to differences as well as recurring problems. DOI 10.1017/S0010417500000037.

sources.title: Richard Grove, Editorial, Environment and History 1(1) (1995), 1–2
sources.note: Complete two-page founding editorial read. Describes planning with Ramachandra Guha, connections to history from below and material culture, and a geographically broad programme complementing existing North American venues. An incidental erroneous Silent Spring date is not used.

sources.title: John Hutchinson, Nations and Nationalism: the first 25 years, Nations and Nationalism 25(1) (2019), 5–15
sources.note: Founding section of the accepted manuscript read, including the reproduced 1995 editorial aims: a research forum consolidating an interdisciplinary scholarly community. Separates ASEN’s earlier formation from the 1995 journal launch. DOI 10.1111/nana.12489.

sources.title: G. E. Gorman, review of Holocaust and Genocide Studies volume 1 (1986), ANZTLA newsletter, p. 19
sources.note: One-page scan read visually. Contemporary review identifies the first volume, institutional associations, and editors’ interdisciplinary Holocaust-and-genocide programme. Reviewer speculation about future coverage and judgments of quality are not adopted; newsletter issue date not established from the isolated page.

sources.title: Steven Seidenberg, review of History and Anthropology volume 1, Journal of the Anthropological Society of Oxford 17(3) (1986), 262–264
sources.note: Read pp. 262–264 from the full reviews-section PDF, including the quoted editorial aims and the 1984 first-part imprint. ORA hosts this multi-review scan under a different review’s metadata; Seidenberg’s name and pages were checked in the document itself.

edges.relationship: First published in 1972 to develop feminist scholarship in conversation with the women’s movement, including historical research and early Berkshire Conference issues.
edges.evidence_note: An interdisciplinary women’s-studies institution with a documented women’s-history component. The edge does not restrict its programme to history or date the origin of women’s history to 1972; organizing began in 1969.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1975 to provide an interdisciplinary forum for the expanding scholarship on women, including historical inquiry and documentary recovery.
edges.evidence_note: Links the historical component of a broader feminist scholarly programme. This is neither a claim of exclusive disciplinary affiliation nor an origin date for all women’s history.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1976 as an institutional forum for historical explanation drawing selectively on social-science theories and methods.
edges.evidence_note: An institutional project within the broad social-history expansion, with qualitative as well as quantitative methods. Its interdisciplinary scope exceeds this atlas entry; it does not endorse every approach listed in the entry.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1927 to develop economic and social historical inquiry, articulated in the first issue through Ashley’s programme and the journal’s original subtitle.
edges.evidence_note: Consolidates an existing field through a society journal. The programme included social history and cannot be reduced to later cliometrics; 1926 is the society’s foundation, not this first publication date.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1973 as an annual forum combining Oral History Association colloquium papers and contributed articles for the developing practice of oral history.
edges.evidence_note: One institutional forum in a much older and internationally diverse practice. The US association, its newsletter and the separate British journal Oral History are not conflated.

edges.relationship: Founded in 1974 as a methodological forum for African history, emphasizing critical scrutiny of historical sources and the ways historians use them.
edges.evidence_note: A specific source-critical programme within African historiography, not the creation of African historical thought or an assignment of every African historian to one method. Claim limited to the available first-editorial extract.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1989 to make gender’s historical experience and significance a focused programme of historical inquiry.
edges.evidence_note: Retrospective abstract-level evidence supports this limited founding-purpose claim. The target is the gender-history component of the combined Gender & racial formation entry; the edge does not date or subsume every racial-formation approach.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1970 to develop interdisciplinary historical methods, giving quantitative analysis a place within a wider exchange with the social sciences and other disciplines.
edges.evidence_note: The quantitative connection is one explicit component of a broader founding programme. The journal is not exclusively quantitative and the link does not equate its programme with all cliometric or serial-history approaches.

edges.relationship: Established as a project in 1912 to institutionalize history of science through Sarton’s programme of historical synthesis, set out in the first volume published in 1913.
edges.evidence_note: Preserves the existing 1912 foundation date and explicitly distinguishes 1913 first publication. The initial Sartonian synthesis is one programme within history of science; it does not characterize the entire field or the journal’s later pluralism.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1958 to create a forum for comparative inquiry across history and the social sciences, bringing specialists into discussion of recurring historical problems.
edges.evidence_note: Its comparative programme offers an institutional home for historical sociology but extends to anthropology and the humanities. The edge neither reduces the journal to sociology nor assigns it the later state-formation theories in this atlas entry.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1995 to broaden environmental history’s geographical and disciplinary conversation, including work on Africa, Asia and other regions alongside Europe and North America.
edges.evidence_note: An expansion and consolidation project in an already established field. Its explicit geographical ambitions provide evidence against treating North American environmental-history venues as the field’s whole institutional history.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1995 to consolidate interdisciplinary research and scholarly exchange on nations and nationalism through an association journal.
edges.evidence_note: A field-consolidating institution after earlier decades of nationalism scholarship, not the field’s beginning or an endorsement of a single explanation of nations.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1986 to provide an interdisciplinary forum for Holocaust research in conversation with the wider scholarly study of genocide.
edges.evidence_note: The edge connects the Holocaust component of a wider programme to the existing atlas entry. Comparative genocide studies is not thereby claimed to be comprehensively represented by that entry; the evidence is contemporary reception, not a full reading of the founding editorial.

edges.relationship: Launched in 1984 to bring historians and anthropologists into a shared forum where each discipline could reconsider its methods through the other’s work.
edges.evidence_note: A particular institutional exchange, not the origin of historical anthropology. Distinct from Stocking’s History of Anthropology series, which the same contemporary review contrasts with this journal; intended collaboration does not prove that disciplinary divisions disappeared.

journal_b37c47d6d6bf8912.note: First publication in 1973 documented by the contemporary OHA launch notice. The included 1972 colloquium is not the publication start. Cessation and present continuity remain unverified.

journal_55b2862e091c93c6.note: First volume and founding editorial published in 1974. Existing library format/end observations remain attributed evidence; no cessation or present continuity is inferred.
